title: Additive equation for a smooth vector hypersurface
statement: Let $k$ be a field of prime characteristic $p>0$ [def-weil-field], let $n\geq1$, and put $E=\mathbf G_a^n$ with coordinatewise addition [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $H\subseteq E$ be a smooth closed subgroup scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-weil-finite-type-morphism, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Suppose $\dim H=n-1$, where dimension is topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]. There exist finitely many coefficients $c_{ij}\in k$, indexed by $1\leq i\leq n$ and $j\geq0$, such that $P=\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_i^{p^j}\in k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ is nonzero, some $c_{i0}$ is nonzero, and $H=\operatorname{Spec}(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(P))$ as a closed subgroup scheme of $E$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum, def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring, def-weil-pbc-algebra-hom-quotient]. Equivalently $H$ is the scheme-theoretic kernel of the $k$-group homomorphism $P:E\to\mathbf G_a$. The polynomial identity $P(X+Y)=P(X)+P(Y)$ holds over $k$. Neither connectedness of $H$ nor perfectness of $k$ is assumed.

source.place: Corollary 1.8 and Propositions 1.6--1.7, printed p.5 (the nonzero linear coefficient expresses separability for a p-polynomial). Read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; WANTED locally. No Stacks tag is claimed for this algebraic-group result.

proof.text: Put $A=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$. By the affine quotient description of a closed immersion write $H=\operatorname{Spec}B$ with $B=A/I$. The identity lies in $H$, so $I\ne A$ and every element of $I$ vanishes at $0$. Smoothness implies reducedness by [lem-trf-smooth-geometrically-normal] (take the extension $k/k$). Thus $I$ is radical: if $a^m\in I$, the class of $a$ is nilpotent in $B$, hence zero. The ring $A$ is Noetherian by [lem-wf-affine-noetherian-components], since its finitely many coordinates generate it over $k$.

source.place: Corollary 1.8 and Proposition 1.7, printed p.5, read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; Proposition 1.6 for the polynomial form. The proof below gives a scheme-theoretic coefficient version of the translation argument, with generic algebra inputs cited separately. Archival copy WANTED locally.

proof.text: For a prime $\mathfrak q$ minimal over $I$, let $\bar{\mathfrak q}=\mathfrak q/I$ in $B$. Its height is zero, because no prime of $B$ is strictly contained in it. The group case of [lem-sfb-field-groupoid-constant-local-dimension] gives $\dim_{\bar{\mathfrak q}}H=\dim H=n-1$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-polynomial-quotient-dimension-at-point-height-difference] to $A\twoheadrightarrow B$: $n-1=n-\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak q)+0$, so $\mathfrak q$ has height one. By [lem-sfb-polynomial-field-ufd], factor any nonzero element of $\mathfrak q$ into primes. One factor $\pi$ belongs to $\mathfrak q$. The ideal $(\pi)$ is a nonzero prime ideal: $ab\in(\pi)$ means $\pi\mid ab$, hence $\pi\mid a$ or $\pi\mid b$. Height one forces $(\pi)=\mathfrak q$. Apply [lem-sfb-radical-prime-generator-principality] to obtain $0\ne P\in A$ with $I=(P)$. Consequently $P(0)=0$ and $d=\deg P\geq1$.

source.place: Corollary 1.8 and Proposition 1.7, printed p.5, read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; Proposition 1.6 for the polynomial form. The proof below gives a scheme-theoretic coefficient version of the translation argument, with generic algebra inputs cited separately. Archival copy WANTED locally.

proof.text: Write $C=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_n]/(P(Y))$ and $\bar Y$ for the residue classes. In the $k$-algebra $C[X]/(P(X))$, both tuples $X$ and $\bar Y$ are points of $H$. Closure under addition therefore gives $P(X+\bar Y)=0$. The quotient kernel says $P(X+\bar Y)=P(X)Q(X)$ in $C[X]$. Order the $X$-monomials by graded lexicographic order. A leading coefficient of $P(X)$ is a nonzero element of $k$, hence a unit in $C$; $C\ne0$ because $P(0)=0$. Translation by $\bar Y$ leaves the leading $X$-monomial and its coefficient unchanged. For any nonzero $Q$, the leading monomial of $P Q$ is the product of the leading monomials: its coefficient is the leading coefficient of $Q$ multiplied by that unit, so cannot vanish. Comparing in the displayed equality forces the leading monomial of $Q$ to be $1$ and its coefficient to be $1$. Hence $Q=1$ and $P(X+\bar Y)=P(X)$. This calculation uses arbitrary algebra points, not just $k$-rational points.

source.place: Corollary 1.8 and Proposition 1.7, printed p.5, read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; Proposition 1.6 for the polynomial form. The proof below gives a scheme-theoretic coefficient version of the translation argument, with generic algebra inputs cited separately. Archival copy WANTED locally.

proof.text: The preceding identity says that every coefficient in $X$ of $P(X+Y)-P(X)$ belongs to $(P(Y))$. Subtracting $P(Y)$, there is $V\in k[X,Y]$ with $D:=P(X+Y)-P(X)-P(Y)=P(Y)V$. The homogeneous part of degree $d$ in the $Y$ variables of $P(X+Y)$ is exactly the top homogeneous part of $P(Y)$, so $D$ has $Y$-degree strictly less than $d$, unless it is zero. If $V\ne0$, multiplication by $P(Y)$ has $Y$-degree $d+\deg_Y V$: the top homogeneous parts have nonzero product in the polynomial ring over the domain $k[X]$. This contradicts the preceding bound. Thus $D=0$, proving $P(X+Y)=P(X)+P(Y)$ over $k$.

source.place: Corollary 1.8 and Proposition 1.7, printed p.5, read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; Proposition 1.6 for the polynomial form. The proof below gives a scheme-theoretic coefficient version of the translation argument, with generic algebra inputs cited separately. Archival copy WANTED locally.

proof.text: Decompose $P=\sum_{r\geq1}P_r$ by total monomial degree; the sum is finite and has no constant term. Substitution $X\mapsto X+Y$ preserves total degree in the joint variables, so comparison of equal-degree monomials in the additive identity gives $P_r(X+Y)=P_r(X)+P_r(Y)$ for each $r$. Apply [lem-trf-additive-polynomial-monomial-classification] to every nonzero homogeneous piece: in characteristic $p$, its degree is $p^j$ for some $j\geq0$ and it has the form $\sum_i c_{ij}x_i^{p^j}$. Summing these finitely many pieces gives the required form of the same polynomial $P$, still generating $I$.

source.place: Corollary 1.8 and Proposition 1.7, printed p.5, read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; Proposition 1.6 for the polynomial form. The proof below gives a scheme-theoretic coefficient version of the translation argument, with generic algebra inputs cited separately. Archival copy WANTED locally.

proof.text: Choose an algebraic closure $K/k$. The affine base change is $H_K=\operatorname{Spec}K[x]/(P)$; it is smooth by the smooth clause of [lem-pc-proper-base-change], and its dimension is $n-1$ by [lem-pc-dim-base-change] applied to the finite-type algebra $B$. By [lem-sfb-group-tangent-dimension-smoothness], its tangent space at $0$ has dimension $n-1$. A tangent vector is a tuple $(a_i\epsilon)$ over $K[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)$ by [def-sc-scheme-tangent-space]. Evaluating the equation gives $P(a\epsilon)=\epsilon\sum_i c_{i0}a_i$, since $p^j\geq2$ for $j>0$. If every $c_{i0}$ were zero, every $a\in K^n$ would be a tangent vector, giving dimension $n$, a contradiction. Thus some $c_{i0}\ne0$. This tests smoothness of the actual quotient scheme, and does not assume that $k$ is perfect.

source.place: Corollary 1.8 and Proposition 1.7, printed p.5, read online at https://math.stanford.edu/~conrad/papers/appbnew.pdf; Proposition 1.6 for the polynomial form. The proof below gives a scheme-theoretic coefficient version of the translation argument, with generic algebra inputs cited separately. Archival copy WANTED locally.

proof.text: The polynomial defines a $k$-scheme map $E\to\mathbf G_a$. The additive identity shows on every $k$-algebra that it preserves addition; $P(0)=0$ gives the identity and $0=P(X-X)=P(X)+P(-X)$ gives inverses. It is therefore a group homomorphism. Its scheme-theoretic kernel has coordinate algebra $k[x]/(P)$: a map from any $k$-algebra factors through that quotient exactly when its tuple is annihilated by $P$. Since $I=(P)$, this is $H$ with its given embedding in $E$. All conclusions, including the closed subgroup scheme equality, follow.
